about: In the prayers at the foot of the altar, Psalm 42 is said alternately by the priest and server. The antiphon “Introíbo ad altáre Dei” precedes it and is repeated after the doxology.

s01.narrative: This part is left out at Requiem Masses, and in Masses of the season from Passion Sunday through Maundy Thursday. What goes is the psalm together with the Glória Patri and the repetition of the antiphon. The rest of the prayers at the foot stay — the sign of the cross, the antiphon and the Adiutórium — and the confession follows at once.

s02.narrative: The priest says the psalm alternately with the server, verse for verse. At a dialogue Mass the faithful answer with the server.

s03.translation: Judge me, O God, and set my cause apart from an unholy nation: from the unjust and deceitful man deliver me.

s04.translation: For Thou art my strength, O God: why hast Thou cast me off, and why do I go about in sadness while the enemy afflicts me?

s05.translation: Send forth Thy light and Thy truth: they have led me and brought me to Thy holy mountain and into Thy tabernacles.

s06.translation: And I will go in unto the altar of God: to God, who gladdens my youth.

s07.translation: I will praise Thee on the harp, O God, my God: why art thou sad, my soul, and why dost thou disquiet me?

s08.translation: Hope in God, for I will praise Him still: the salvation of my countenance, and my God.

s09.translation: Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.

s10.translation: As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end. Amen.

s11.narrative: The psalm ended, the priest takes up the antiphon once more — as in the Office an antiphon returns after the psalm it framed.

s12.translation: I will go in unto the altar of God.

s13.translation: To God, who gladdens my youth.

w002.function: Accusative — the object of the imperative “Iúdica” (w001). The bare form could also be ablative. The verb settles it.

w003.function: Vocative, though the form is the same as the nominative: for deus the nominative serves as the address. That this is address is shown by the imperative beside it.

w006.function: A term from the courts: a causa is a case pleaded before a judge. The psalmist asks for a verdict, not for pity.

w011.function: Agrees with “gente” (w009), so ablative and not nominative — “non sancta” is one description: an unholy nation.

w013.function: Ablative after “ab” (w012). The singular here covers any such man.

w014.function: Agrees with “hómine” (w013). The bare form could also be dative.

w016.function: Agrees with “hómine” (w013) — the second of the two descriptions.

w017.function: Literally to dig out, to grub up — a strong word, as though someone had to be got out from under the ground.

w020.function: The pronoun is not needed — the ending of “es” (w021) already says who. It stands to press the point: thou, and no other.

w023.function: The predicate of “es” (w021), and therefore nominative: thou art my strength.

w024.function: Agrees with “fortitúdo” (w023) — nominative. The same form is ablative in the Confiteor's “mea culpa”.

w027.function: Perfect: the thing is done and its effect lasts — hence the question.

w030.function: This sentence does not determine whether the form is masculine or feminine.

w031.function: Not simply “I go”: the verb names a manner of walking, here the gait of a man weighed down.

w035.function: An adjective used as a noun — the unfriendly man, the enemy. Here the subject of the clause.

w042.function: Neuter plural, although it stands for two feminine nouns: “lucem” (w037) and “veritátem” (w040). The Greek psalter has neuter αὐτά here, because the first of its two nouns (φῶς, light) is neuter — the Latin followed the Greek and not its own genders.

w044.function: Plural: the subject is two gifts — light and truth — acting together.

w047.function: With the accusative — motion toward. The same preposition with the ablative would mean being there already.

w048.function: The temple hill: the end of the pilgrimage the psalmist is making.

w053.function: Accusative plural after “in” (w052) — motion toward again. Tents, not a building: the word remembers the tabernacle in the desert.

w056.function: This verse is the antiphon of this psalm: the liturgy lifted it out and set it before the psalm and after it.

w059.function: A genitive dependent on “altáre” (w058): the altar of God.

w062.function: Nominative, though its antecedent “Deum” (w061) stands in the accusative: a relative takes its case from its own clause, where it is the subject.

w064.function: The Hebrew has two words for joy here and none meaning youth. The Greek translation reads “youth”, and the Latin follows the Greek.

w066.function: The same verb opens the Confiteor, but means something else here: not to own a fault but to praise. Both senses live in confitéri — to declare openly, whether a sin or the glory of God.

w067.function: Dative: confitéri governs the dative of the person — to declare to someone.

w069.function: Ablative after “in” (w068) — to its accompaniment. The spelling does not distinguish nominative from ablative here. The preposition settles it.

w071.function: Repeating the name is a Hebrew way of intensifying: not two invocations but one made stronger.

w072.function: Nominative, though the phrase addresses: the masculine has no vocative but “mi”, which the psalter does not use here. Unlike “mea” (w077), where vocative and nominative sound alike.

w076.function: Vocative: the psalmist turns and addresses his own soul as another person. The form is the same as the nominative and the ablative.

w082.function: An imperative addressed to ánima mea in the preceding sentence.

w084.function: Ablative after “in” (w083). The same form opens the Confiteor as a dative — I confess to God. Here it is the thing hope rests on.

w088.function: Dative with “confitébor” (w087) — to declare to someone. The bare form can also be a masculine nominative plural.

w089.function: The adjective salutáris used as a noun: the thing that saves. It stands in the nominative although “illi” (w088) was dative — the sentence changes construction in mid course, and so does the Greek behind it.

w090.function: A 4th-declension genitive, shaped like the nominative — “mei” (w091) shows which it is. Vultus is the face as it looks out — the gaze turned toward someone.

w093.function: Nominative here, not vocative: it stands beside “salutáre” (w089) as the second member of the same phrase. In the verse before, the same form was a vocative.

w095.function: A nominative with no verb: a sentence of wish whose “be” was never spoken.

w096.function: Dative: to whom the glory goes.

w111.function: The same preposition that stood a moment ago before “princípio” (w105), but there with the ablative and here with the accusative: there the time in which something was, here the time toward which it runs.

w113.function: A genitive beside the same noun in the accusative: ages of ages — the Hebrew way of saying what has no end.

w115.function: The antiphon returns after the psalm and its doxology, as in the Office it returns after the psalm it framed.
